title: Exercise: structure — symmetric, banded, sparse
Exercise: structure — symmetric, banded, sparse
text:
By hand
B1. Cholesky. (a) Compute the Cholesky factor \(L\) of the covariance matrix of three genes \[\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 10 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & 6 \end{pmatrix}.\] (b) Use \(L\) to solve \(\Sigma\mathbf{x} = (4, 14, 6)^T\): first \(L\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}\), then \(L^T\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}\). (c) Compute \(\det\Sigma\) from \(L\). Check it with the usual 3 × 3 determinant formula. (d) Three genes have pairwise correlations estimated from different subsets of samples (missing values): \(r_{12} = 0.9\), \(r_{13} = 0.9\), \(r_{23} = -0.9\). Try to compute the Cholesky factor of the correlation matrix. Where does it break? Explain in words why these three correlations cannot all be true at once.
B2. Thomas by hand. Four cells with \(D = 1\), \(k = 1\) and production 1 in cell 1: \[\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\mathbf{c} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}.\] (a) Write down the vectors \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), \(d\) (with \(a_1\) and \(c_4\) unused). (b) Run the forward sweep with fractions: give the new \(b_2, b_3, b_4\) and \(d_2, d_3, d_4\). (c) Back-substitute to get \(c_4, c_3, c_2, c_1\). (d) Check mass balance: total degradation \(k\sum_i c_i\) should equal total production. Is it? (e) Is the matrix diagonally dominant? Are all pivots (\(b_1\) and the new \(b_2, b_3, b_4\)) positive?
B3. When Thomas breaks. (a) Run the forward sweep for \(a = (\cdot, 1, 1)\), \(b = (1, 1, 1)\), \(c = (1, 1, \cdot)\). What happens at the second pivot? (b) Is this matrix diagonally dominant? Is it singular? (Compute its determinant.) (c) Which algorithm from Pivoting, norms and conditioning would solve it, and why?
B4. CSC by hand. A count matrix of 3 genes × 5 cells: \[M = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.\] (a) Write down x, i and p (0-based, column by column). (b) Use only x and p to compute the total count (library size) of each cell. (c) Go back: which matrix (3 × 3) has x = (5, 1, 2), i = (2, 0, 1), p = (0, 1, 1, 3)? (d) A 20 000 genes × 100 000 cells matrix has 7 % non-zeros. How much memory does it take dense, and in CSC (8 bytes per value, 4 per row index and per pointer)? Above what fraction of non-zeros is CSC larger than dense?
B5. Fill-in. Use only the pattern: write × for a non-zero and · for a zero. (a) The arrow matrix with the hub first: \[A = \begin{pmatrix} \times & \times & \times & \times \\ \times & \times & \cdot & \cdot \\ \times & \cdot & \times & \cdot \\ \times & \cdot & \cdot & \times \end{pmatrix}.\] Eliminate the first column (subtract multiples of row 1 from rows 2–4). Which zeros become non-zero? What is the pattern of \(L\)? (b) Renumber so the hub is last. Write the new pattern and eliminate. How many fill-ins now? (c) Does elimination of a tridiagonal matrix (Thomas) create any fill-in? (d) Compute the inverse of \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) (hint: check that it is \(\tfrac14\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}\)). How many zeros does it have?
B6. Jacobi by hand. (a) Do two Jacobi steps from \(\mathbf{x} = (0, 0)\) for \(\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\mathbf{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}\). Compare with the exact solution \((1/11, 7/11)\). (b) Do three Jacobi steps from \((0, 0)\) for \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\mathbf{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}\) (exact solution \((1, 1)\)). What happens? Which of the two matrices is diagonally dominant?
B7. What structure buys. A computer does \(10^9\) operations per second. (a) For a row of \(n = 10^4\) cells, estimate the time of dense LU (\(\tfrac23 n^3\)), dense Cholesky (\(\tfrac13 n^3\)) and Thomas (\(8n\)). (b) Memory of the dense matrix and of the three diagonals, in bytes. (c) Same for \(n = 10^6\).

title: Exercise: structure — symmetric, banded, sparse
text:
In code
C1. Cholesky. Check B1 (a)–(d) in code: the factor, the two triangular solves (R: forwardsolve / backsolve; Python: scipy.linalg.solve_triangular), the log-determinant, and the failure for the correlation matrix of B1(d). Print the eigenvalues of that matrix.
C2. Log-determinant of an LD matrix. The correlation between \(n = 2000\) equally spaced SNP markers is \(\Sigma_{ij} = 0.9^{|i-j|}\). (a) Compute det(S) and the log-determinant from the Cholesky factor. Compare with determinant(S, logarithm = TRUE) (Python: np.linalg.slogdet) and with the exact value \((n-1)\log(1 - 0.9^2)\). (b) The quadratic form of the log-likelihood is \(\mathbf{y}^T\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{y}\). With \(\mathbf{z} = L^{-1}\mathbf{y}\) it is \(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\). Compute it for \(\mathbf{y} = (1, \dots, 1)\) with one triangular solve, and check against a general solve and the exact value \(\big(2 + (n-2)(1+\rho^2) - 2(n-1)\rho\big)/(1-\rho^2)\).
C3. The Thomas algorithm. Write thomas(a, b, c, d) (convention as in the lecture: all four vectors of length \(n\)). (a) Check your answer to B2. (b) Solve the morphogen system for \(n = 100\) cells and check it three ways: the residual \(\max|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{s}|\), mass balance \(k\sum x_i = 1\), and \(x_{11}/x_1 \approx e^{-1}\) (decay length 10 cells). (c) Compare with a library solver: R Matrix::bandSparse + solve, Python scipy.linalg.solve_banded.
C4. Timing. Time a dense solve and thomas for \(n = 1000, 2000, 4000\) cells, and thomas alone for \(n = 10^5\) and \(10^6\). By what factor does each time grow when \(n\) doubles? Extrapolate the dense solve to \(10^6\) cells.
C5. Thomas without pivoting. (a) Write diag_dominant(a, b, c). Apply it to the morphogen matrix and to \(a = (\cdot, 1, 1, 1)\), \(b = (10^{-17}, 2, 2, 2)\), \(c = (1, 1, 1, \cdot)\). (b) Solve the second system with d = (1, 1, 1, 1) by thomas and by a general solver. Compute the residual of the Thomas answer. What went wrong?
C6. CSC and the dense inverse. (a) Build \(M\) from B4 from triplets (R sparseMatrix, Python scipy.sparse.csc_matrix, Rust sprs::TriMat) and print its three arrays (R: M@x, M@i, M@p; Python: .data, .indices, .indptr). Compare with B4(a). Compute the library sizes. (b) For the 100-cell morphogen matrix, count the non-zeros of \(A\) and of \(A^{-1}\) (Python: scipy.sparse.linalg.inv). What would \(A^{-1}\) cost in memory for \(10^6\) cells?
C7. Fill-in. Build the 1000 × 1000 arrow matrix (hub gene: diagonal \(n\), row and column of ones; other genes: diagonal 2) with the hub first and with the hub last. Count the non-zeros of the Cholesky factor in both cases. In R, also try Cholesky(A, perm = TRUE). (Python: scipy has no sparse Cholesky; use scipy.sparse.linalg.splu with permc_spec="NATURAL" and "COLAMD".)
C8. Jacobi and conjugate gradient. Write jacobi(A, b, tol, maxit) and cg(A, b, tol, maxit) that stop when \(\|\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}\| <\) tol and report the number of iterations (or that they did not converge). (a) Run both on the morphogen system with \(n = 1000\) cells and tol = 1e-10. How many iterations does each need? How close are they to the direct solution? (Python: compare with scipy.sparse.linalg.cg.) (b) Run Jacobi on the matrix of B6(b) for 50 iterations. What happens?

title: Exercise: structure — symmetric, banded, sparse
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — Cholesky by hand (B1)





Work column by column. Column 1: \(\ell_{11} = \sqrt{a_{11}}\), then \(\ell_{i1} = a_{i1}/\ell_{11}\). Column 2: \(\ell_{22} = \sqrt{a_{22} - \ell_{21}^2}\), \(\ell_{32} = (a_{32} - \ell_{31}\ell_{21})/\ell_{22}\). Column 3: \(\ell_{33} = \sqrt{a_{33} - \ell_{31}^2 - \ell_{32}^2}\). For (c), \(\det\Sigma = \det L \cdot \det L^T = (\ell_{11}\ell_{22}\ell_{33})^2\).









Hint 2 — Thomas (B2, C3)





Keep fractions: \(b_2 = 3 - \tfrac{-1}{2}(-1) = \tfrac52\). The multiplier \(w\) is \(a_i\) divided by the new \(b_{i-1}\). In Python, copy b and d inside the function (b = np.array(b, dtype=float)), otherwise the caller’s arrays are overwritten. To build the matrix for a check: R bandSparse(n, k = -1:1, diagonals = list(a[-1], b, c[-n])); Python scipy.sparse.diags([a[1:], b, c[:-1]], [-1, 0, 1]). For solve_banded((1, 1), ab, d) the rows of ab are the super-diagonal (shifted right by one), the diagonal and the sub-diagonal (shifted left).









Hint 3 — CSC (B4, C6)





Go down column 1 from top to bottom, then column 2, and so on. p starts at 0 and after each column adds the number of non-zeros in that column; an empty column repeats the previous value. Library size of cell \(j\) = sum of x[p[j]] to x[p[j+1]-1].









Hint 4 — fill-in (B5, C7)





Subtracting a multiple of row 1 from row \(i\) makes row \(i\) non-zero wherever row 1 is non-zero. If row 1 is full, every later row becomes full. In code count non-zeros with nnzero (R), .nnz or np.count_nonzero (Python). Build the arrow matrix with Diagonal(n, 2) and forceSymmetric in R, scipy.sparse.lil_matrix in Python.









Hint 5 — Jacobi and CG (B6, C8)





Jacobi: \(x_1^{\text{new}} = (b_1 - a_{12}x_2)/a_{11}\), \(x_2^{\text{new}} = (b_2 - a_{21}x_1)/a_{22}\), using the old \(x\) on the right. CG, one step: \(\alpha = \mathbf{r}^T\mathbf{r} / \mathbf{p}^TA\mathbf{p}\), \(\mathbf{x} \leftarrow \mathbf{x} + \alpha\mathbf{p}\), \(\mathbf{r} \leftarrow \mathbf{r} - \alpha A\mathbf{p}\), \(\mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{r} + (\mathbf{r}^T\mathbf{r})_\text{new}/(\mathbf{r}^T\mathbf{r})_\text{old}\,\mathbf{p}\), starting from \(\mathbf{x} = 0\), \(\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{b}\). With a sparse A, A %*% x (R, returns a 1-column matrix: take [, 1]) and A @ x (Python) cost \(O(\text{nnz})\).

title: Exercise: structure — symmetric, banded, sparse
Exercise: structure — symmetric, banded, sparse
text:
Where this leads

Least squares: normal equations vs QR (Part 4): the normal equations \(X^TX\boldsymbol\beta = X^T\mathbf{y}\) have an SPD matrix and are solved by Cholesky, but squaring \(X\) squares the condition number.
How eigen() works, and big problems (Part 5): PCA of a sparse single-cell matrix with Krylov methods (irlba, scipy.sparse.linalg.eigsh), which, like CG, only need products \(A\mathbf{x}\).
Implicit schemes and the method of lines (Part 10): one Thomas solve per time step for diffusion along a line; Steady state in two dimensions (Part 10): sparse matrices from Kronecker products and sparse direct solves with fill-reducing orderings.
Iterative linear solvers in depth (Part 11, optional): Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel, conjugate gradient, GMRES and preconditioning for systems too large for a direct solve.

title: Quiz: structure — symmetric, banded, sparse
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of Cholesky, tridiagonal and sparse solvers. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Which of these matrices are symmetric positive definite? (a) The sample covariance of 5 genes measured in 3 samples. (b) The identity matrix. (c) \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\). (d) \(0.6\,K + 0.4\,I\), where \(K\) is a kinship matrix estimated from fewer SNPs than individuals.






Hint





SPD means symmetric with all eigenvalues \(> 0\). A covariance matrix estimated from \(m\) samples has rank at most \(m - 1\). Adding \(cI\) raises every eigenvalue by \(c\).









Answer






No: rank at most 2, so three of the five eigenvalues are 0 (semidefinite, not definite). (b) Yes, all eigenvalues 1. (c) No: eigenvalues 3 and \(-1\). (d) Yes: \(K\) is semidefinite (eigenvalues \(\ge 0\)), and \(0.4I\) raises them all to at least \(0.4\). This is why mixed models with a residual variance are always solvable by Cholesky.





Q2. Give two reasons to use Cholesky rather than LU for an SPD matrix.






Hint





Count operations, and think about what pivoting is for.









Answer





It costs half as much (\(\tfrac13 n^3\) against \(\tfrac23 n^3\)) and stores one triangle, and it needs no pivoting: for an SPD matrix the entries of \(L\) cannot grow (\(\ell_{ij}^2 \le a_{ii}\)), so it is stable as it stands. A third: it is the cheapest test of positive definiteness, and it gives \(\log\det A = 2\sum\log\ell_{ii}\) for free.




Q3. R stops with the leading minor of order 5 is not positive when you call chol() on a 200 × 200 gene covariance matrix. What does this mean, and what can you do?






Hint





Where in the algorithm can Cholesky fail? How many samples went into the covariance?









Answer





At column 5 the number under the square root was \(\le 0\): the matrix is not positive definite (in practice, the covariance was estimated from fewer samples than genes, or assembled from pairwise correlations, so it is singular or has negative eigenvalues). Options: more samples; shrinkage \(C + \lambda I\) (or \((1-\alpha)C + \alpha\,\mathrm{diag}(C)\)); a model with an explicit error variance; or work with fewer genes. Check with the smallest eigenvalue.




Q4. Why compute the log-determinant of a 5000 × 5000 covariance matrix as 2 * sum(log(diag(chol(S)))) rather than log(det(S))?






Hint





What is the determinant of a large matrix with eigenvalues below 1? Recall How computers store numbers.









Answer





The determinant is a product of 5000 numbers (eigenvalues, or squared \(\ell_{ii}\)); if they are typically below 1 it underflows to 0 (above 1 it overflows to Inf), and the log is -Inf (or Inf). The sum of logs is an ordinary number. Same idea as summing log-likelihoods instead of multiplying likelihoods. (determinant(S, logarithm = TRUE) and np.linalg.slogdet also work.)




Q5. To simulate expression of three genes with covariance \(\Sigma\), a colleague writes R <- chol(Sigma); y <- R %*% z with z <- rnorm(3). What is wrong? Check by computing the covariance of y.






Hint





Which triangle does R’s chol return? \(\operatorname{Cov}(M\mathbf{z}) = MM^T\).









Answer





R’s chol returns the upper factor \(R = L^T\), so \(\operatorname{Cov}(R\mathbf{z}) = RR^T = L^TL\), which is not \(\Sigma\). Use t(R) %*% z. (In numpy and nalgebra the factor is already the lower \(L\), so L @ z is right; code translated between the languages often gets this wrong.)

RPythonRust


Sigma <- matrix(c(4, 2, -2,  2, 10, 2,  -2, 2, 6), nrow = 3)
R <- chol(Sigma)
R %*% t(R)                               # covariance of R %*% z: wrong
#      [,1] [,2] [,3]
# [1,]    6    2   -2
# [2,]    2   10    2
# [3,]   -2    2    4
t(R) %*% R                               # covariance of t(R) %*% z: Sigma
#      [,1] [,2] [,3]
# [1,]    4    2   -2
# [2,]    2   10    2
# [3,]   -2    2    6


import numpy as np
Sigma = np.array([[4.0, 2, -2], [2, 10, 2], [-2, 2, 6]])
L = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma)        # numpy: lower factor
R = L.T                              # what R's chol() returns
print(R @ R.T)                       # covariance of R @ z: wrong
# [[ 6.  2. -2.]
#  [ 2. 10.  2.]
#  [-2.  2.  4.]]
print(L @ L.T)                       # covariance of L @ z: Sigma
# [[ 4.  2. -2.]
#  [ 2. 10.  2.]
#  [-2.  2.  6.]]


// rust/examples/structured_sparse_q5.rs  —  cargo run --example structured_sparse_q5
// Q5: which triangle? R's chol() returns the upper factor R = L^T.
use nalgebra::dmatrix;

fn main() {
    let sigma = dmatrix![4.0, 2.0, -2.0; 2.0, 10.0, 2.0; -2.0, 2.0, 6.0];
    let l = sigma.cholesky().unwrap().l();   // nalgebra: lower factor
    let r = l.transpose();                   // what R's chol() returns
    println!("{}", &r * r.transpose());      // covariance of R z: wrong
    println!("{}", &l * l.transpose());      // covariance of L z: Sigma
}

// Output:
//   ┌          ┐
//   │  6  2 -2 │
//   │  2 10  2 │
//   │ -2  2  4 │
//   └          ┘
//   ┌          ┐
//   │  4  2 -2 │
//   │  2 10  2 │
//   │ -2  2  6 │
//   └          ┘







Q6. Thomas solves the morphogen system for \(10^5\) cells in 0.05 s. Roughly how long for \(10^6\) cells? A dense solve() takes 1 s for 4000 cells; roughly how long for 8000?






Hint





Thomas is \(O(n)\), dense LU \(O(n^3)\).









Answer





Thomas: 10 times more cells, 10 times longer, about 0.5 s. Dense: twice the size, \(2^3 = 8\) times longer, about 8 s (in practice 6–8 s; small sizes have overheads).




Q7. Is the Thomas algorithm safe for a tridiagonal matrix with diagonal 1 and off-diagonals \(-0.8\) (above and below)? And with diagonal 2.01 and off-diagonals \(-1\)? What should you check after solving?






Hint





Compare \(|b_i|\) with \(|a_i| + |c_i|\).









Answer





First matrix: \(1 < 0.8 + 0.8\), not diagonally dominant, so there is no guarantee: a pivot may come close to zero (it is not SPD either: its smallest eigenvalue, about \(1 - 1.6\), is negative for large \(n\)). Second: \(2.01 > 2\), diagonally dominant, safe. In both cases, check the residual \(\max|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{d}|\) after solving, and switch to a solver with pivoting (solve, scipy.linalg.solve_banded) if it is large.




Q8. A sparse matrix in CSC has x = (2, 1, 4, 3), i = (0, 2, 1, 2), p = (0, 2, 2, 4). Write it out. How many columns does it have, and which one is empty?






Hint





p has one more entry than there are columns. Column \(j\) (from 0) has entries p[j] to p[j+1] - 1.









Answer





Three columns. Column 0: entries 0–1, values 2 (row 0) and 1 (row 2). Column 1: p[1] = p[2], empty. Column 2: entries 2–3, values 4 (row 1) and 3 (row 2). \[\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\]




Q9. Your sparse 10⁶ × 10⁶ tridiagonal matrix takes 36 MB. Why does solve(A) %*% b run out of memory when solve(A, b) takes half a second?






Hint





How many zeros does the inverse of a tridiagonal matrix have?









Answer





The inverse of a (connected) sparse matrix is in general dense: every cell influences every other, so \(A^{-1}\) has \(10^{12}\) non-zero entries, 8 TB. solve(A, b) factorises \(A\), and the factors of a tridiagonal matrix stay tridiagonal (no fill-in), then solves: \(O(n)\) time and memory.




Q10. In a gene network one transcription factor is linked to all 5000 other genes, which are otherwise unlinked. You factorise its sparse precision matrix by Cholesky. Should the hub be the first or the last unknown? What happens in the other case?






Hint





Eliminating an unknown connects all of its neighbours to each other.









Answer





Last. Eliminating the hub first connects every gene to every other: \(L\) is full, about \(1.25\times10^7\) non-zeros instead of about \(10^4\), and the factorisation costs \(O(n^3)\) instead of \(O(n)\). Sparse solvers choose such an ordering automatically (Matrix::Cholesky(A, perm = TRUE), splu(permc_spec="COLAMD")); check with the number of non-zeros in the factor.




Q11. You run Jacobi on a large sparse system. After 1000 iterations the residual \(\|\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}\|\) has grown from 1 to \(10^{12}\). What is the likely cause, and what are your options?






Hint





When is Jacobi guaranteed to converge? What does CG need?









Answer





\(A\) is probably not diagonally dominant, and the Jacobi iteration matrix \(I - D^{-1}A\) has an eigenvalue larger than 1 in size, so the error grows every step. Options: a sparse direct solve if it fits in memory; conjugate gradient if \(A\) is SPD; GMRES or a preconditioned method otherwise (Iterative linear solvers in depth). In every case, monitor the residual and stop with a message when it does not fall.

title: Exercise: pivoting, norms and conditioning
text:
Explore
The demo below is the two-dye unmixing from the lecture, computed in your browser. Panel (a) shows the two emission spectra (Gaussian, width 30 nm) with the detectors at the peaks; the overlap \(c\) is the signal of dye 2 in detector 1, and the peak spacing follows from it. Panel (b) shows detector readings: 400 simulated cells that all carry 1 unit of each dye, read with independent detector noise (the dashed circle is 2 standard deviations), and one red cell, your cell, whose reading is \(\mathbf b = A(1, 1) + \Delta\mathbf b\). Panel (c) shows the unmixed amounts \(\mathbf x = A^{-1}\mathbf b\): the two equations of your cell as lines (solid: exact \(\mathbf b\); dashed: \(\mathbf b + \Delta\mathbf b\)), their intersection, and the unmixed cloud of cells with its predicted 2-sd ellipse. The readout gives \(A\), its singular values, \(\kappa_2\), your cell’s relative changes (2-norm) and their ratio, and the standard deviation of the unmixed dye 1 over all cells. The cells use a fixed random seed, so you see the same cells every time; the browser computes in the same doubles as R and Python, but the random numbers are not R’s.



E1. (the teaser, as a picture) With \(c = 0.95\), click \(\Delta\mathbf b = (+0.01, -0.01)\). Read off \(\mathbf b\), \(\hat{\mathbf x}\), the two relative changes and the amplification, and compare with \(\kappa\). Then click \((+0.01, +0.01)\). Look at the lines in panel (c): why does the same size of \(\Delta\mathbf b\) move the intersection so far in one case and hardly at all in the other?






Answer E1





\(\Delta\mathbf b = (+0.01, -0.01)\): \(\mathbf b = (1.960, 1.940)\), \(\hat{\mathbf x} = (1.200, 0.800)\), \(\|\Delta\mathbf b\|/\|\mathbf b\| = 0.51\,\%\), \(\|\Delta\mathbf x\|/\|\mathbf x\| = 20.0\,\%\), amplification \(39.0 = \kappa\): the teaser of the lecture, and the worst case. \(\Delta\mathbf b = (+0.01, +0.01)\): \(\hat{\mathbf x} = (1.005, 1.005)\), both relative changes \(0.51\,\%\), amplification \(1.0\). The two lines have slopes \(-1/0.95\) and \(-0.95\): nearly parallel, both along \((1, -1)\). Changing \(\mathbf b\) along \((1, 1)\) shifts both lines the same way, perpendicular to themselves, and the crossing moves only a little along \((1, 1)\). Changing \(\mathbf b\) along \((1, -1)\) shifts them in opposite directions; two nearly parallel lines that move apart a little cross far away, sliding along \((1, -1)\), the squashed direction of the ellipse in the lecture.



E2. (overlap and \(\kappa\)) Keep \(\Delta\mathbf b = (+0.01, -0.01)\) and click \(c = 0.5\), \(0.9\), \(0.95\) and \(0.99\). For each, write down the peak spacing, \(\kappa\), \(\hat{\mathbf x}\) and the amplification. Check \(\kappa = (1+c)/(1-c)\) and \(\Delta\mathbf x = 0.01/(1-c)\cdot(1, -1)\). What does unmixing report for dye 2 at \(c = 0.99\)?

\(\kappa = 1.5/0.5 = 3\), \(1.9/0.1 = 19\), \(1.95/0.05 = 39\), \(1.99/0.01 = 199\); \(\Delta x_1 = 0.01/(1-c) = 0.02, 0.1, 0.2, 1\). The amplification equals \(\kappa\) every time, because this \(\Delta\mathbf b\) is the worst direction and \(\mathbf b \propto (1, 1)\) the best. At \(c = 0.99\) a 0.5 % detector error turns a cell with 1 unit of each dye into one with 2 units of dye 1 and none of dye 2: the cell would be called dye-2-negative.



E3. (a single noisy detector) Set \(c = 0.95\) and click \(\Delta\mathbf b = (+0.01, 0)\): only detector 1 is off. Read the amplification. Then drag the red point in (b) around the dashed circle and watch the amplification. Where is it largest, where smallest? Is it ever above \(\kappa\)?






Answer E3





\((+0.01, 0)\): \(\hat{\mathbf x} = (1.103, 0.903)\), \(0.36\,\% \to 10.0\,\%\), amplification \(27.6\), between 1 and \(\kappa = 39\). An error in one detector is half “along \((1, 1)\)” and half “along \((1, -1)\)”, and the second half is the one amplified. Dragging around the circle, the amplification is largest (39) when \(\Delta\mathbf b\) points along \((1, -1)\) or \((-1, 1)\) and smallest (1) along \((1, 1)\) or \((-1, -1)\). It never exceeds \(\kappa\): \(\kappa\) is the bound over all directions, reached only in the worst one.



E4. (spillover spreading) Click \(\Delta\mathbf b = 0\) and untick lines, so panel (c) shows only the cells. Click \(c = 0.5\), \(0.9\), \(0.95\), \(0.99\) and read the standard deviation of the unmixed dye 1 each time. What shape does the noise circle in (b) take in (c), and along which direction? Then, at \(c = 0.95\), move the noise sd slider to \(0.005\) and \(0.02\). What does a better detector buy, and what does it not change?






Answer E4





With noise sd \(0.01\): sd of unmixed dye 1 \(= 0.015\), \(0.070\), \(0.140\), \(0.700\) for \(c = 0.5, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99\) (predicted \(0.015\), \(0.071\), \(0.141\), \(0.707\); the factor \(\|\text{row 1 of } A^{-1}\|_2 = \sqrt{1+c^2}/(1-c^2)\) is \(1.5\), \(7.1\), \(14.1\), \(70.7\), as in C7). The round cloud of readings becomes an ellipse along \((1, -1)\), dye 1 against dye 2, with half-axes \(2\sigma/(1-c)\) and \(2\sigma/(1+c)\): the ratio of the axes is exactly \(\kappa\). At \(c = 0.99\), 158 of the 400 cells lie outside the plotted square. At \(c = 0.95\), noise sd \(0.005\) gives sd \(0.070\) and \(0.02\) gives \(0.280\): the spread is proportional to the detector noise, so a better detector shrinks the cloud, but the amplification factor (\(\times 14.1\)) and the shape stay the same. Only the overlap \(c\), that is the choice of dyes, changes \(\kappa\).

title: Exercise: least squares, normal equations vs QR
text:
Explore
The demo below fits a polynomial of degree \(d\) to the standards of the BCA assay or the qPCR curve, in your browser, by both routes: the normal equations (form \(A^TA\) and \(A^T\mathbf b\) in doubles, then Gaussian elimination with pivoting, as solve does) and Householder QR (\(R\mathbf x = Q^T\mathbf b\)). Panel (a) shows the standards, the QR fit (solid), the normal-equations fit (dashed) and the residuals as vertical segments, with a magnified residual strip below. You can drag any standard up or down. Panel (b) shows, for every degree, the relative error \(\|\mathbf x - \mathbf x_\text{exact}\| / \|\mathbf x_\text{exact}\|\) of the coefficients from each route, with the lines \(\kappa^2\varepsilon\) and \(\kappa\varepsilon\) for \(\kappa = \kappa(A)\) in the chosen units. The right-hand axis turns the error into correct digits. The exact least-squares solution is computed in exact fractions (big-integer arithmetic), so the error you see is the rounding error of the route itself. Degrees where \(\kappa(A^TA) = \kappa(A)^2 > 1/\varepsilon\) are shaded: at those degrees R’s solve stops with “computationally singular”. Click a degree in panel (b) to select it.
The browser computes in the same IEEE doubles as R and Python, so \(\kappa\), the coefficients and the RSS agree with the lecture. The last digits of the errors depend on the order of the additions, so your own C5 errors will differ somewhat from the ones shown here, but their size will not.



E1. (choose the degree from the residuals) The demo starts with the BCA standards, \(x\) in mg/mL, and a straight line. Read the RSS and the residual signs. Then move the slider to \(d = 2\) and \(d = 3\). Which degree would you use for the calibration, and why?






Answer E1





\(d = 1\): RSS \(= 0.0573\), signs −−−−−−+++++++++−−−: long runs, the line underestimates the middle and overestimates both ends (lack of fit). \(d = 2\): RSS \(= 5.54\times10^{-3}\), ten times smaller, and the signs alternate without long runs (−−+−−++−+−++−−+−++). \(d = 3\): RSS \(= 4.12\times10^{-3}\), only 25 % smaller than the quadratic, and still no pattern. The quadratic removes the systematic error; the cubic only fits noise a little better. Use \(d = 2\), as in C6.



E2. (the normal equations square κ) Stay in mg/mL. Click degrees 2, 4, 6 and 8 in panel (b). For each, write down \(\kappa(A)\), \(\kappa(A^TA)\) and the correct digits of both routes. How many digits does each route lose compared with 16, and how does that compare with \(\log_{10}\kappa\)?






Answer E2

\(\kappa(A^TA)\) is exactly the square of \(\kappa(A)\). At \(d = 8\), \(\log_{10}\kappa = 7.3\): QR loses 6 digits, close to \(\log_{10}\kappa\), while the normal equations lose 13, close to \(2\log_{10}\kappa = 14.6\). In panel (b) the squares follow the steep \(\kappa^2\varepsilon\) line and the circles the \(\kappa\varepsilon\) line, both a little below it (the lines are worst cases). This is the lecture’s error-versus-\(\kappa\) plot (“Genuine ill-conditioning: digits lost”) with real calibration data. At low degree both routes are fine: the normal equations are only a problem when \(\kappa\) is large.



E3. (units and centring) Set \(d = 3\) and switch to µg/mL. Compare \(\kappa(A)\), the warning and the correct digits with the mg/mL values. Then click degree 8. Finally switch to centred, [−1, 1] and look at \(d = 3\) and \(d = 8\) again. Which change of \(x\) only changes \(\kappa\), and which one actually buys digits?






Answer E3





\(d = 3\) in µg/mL: \(\kappa(A) = 5.78\times10^9\), \(\kappa(A^TA) = 3.34\times10^{19} > 1/\varepsilon\); the readout warns that R’s solve stops here, as on the lecture slide. Yet the computed errors barely move: 13.6 digits (normal equations) and 14.6 (QR), against 14.0 and 15.0 in mg/mL. In panel (b) the dashed lines jump up by many decades while the squares and circles stay put. Columns of very different size are a fake ill-conditioning: rescaling a column only rescales one coefficient, and both elimination with pivoting and Householder QR are hardly affected by it. solve’s check is fooled, though, and so is any \(\kappa\) you compute. At \(d = 8\) the two unit choices are again alike (normal equations 4.2 digits in µg/mL and 3.0 in mg/mL, QR 11.0 and 10.0). Centring is different: with \(t = (x - 1000)/1000\) the columns \(1, t, t^2, \dots\) no longer look alike, and \(\kappa\) drops to 9.3 at \(d = 3\) and to \(4.1\times10^4\) at \(d = 8\) (against \(2.0\times10^7\) in mg/mL). At \(d = 8\) the normal equations now give 8.0 digits instead of 3.0, QR 11.5 instead of 10.0. Rescaling removes the size problem, centring removes part of the look-alike problem; poly() removes all of it.



E4. (the qPCR line) Switch to qPCR (\(x = \log_{10} N\)). Read \(\kappa\) and the RSS at \(d = 1\) and \(d = 2\), then go to \(d = 6\). Then switch to centred at \(d = 6\). Is a curved standard curve justified here?






Answer E4





\(d = 1\): \(\kappa(A) = 10.4\), \(\kappa(A^TA) = 108\), RSS \(= 0.627\) (the lecture’s 10.40 and 0.6266); both routes give 15.7 digits. \(d = 2\): RSS \(= 0.626\), practically unchanged, and the residual signs are the same as for the line: the quadratic term adds nothing. \(d = 6\): \(\kappa = 2.45\times10^7\), normal equations 7.5 digits, QR 11.6, RSS \(0.452\): the curve bends through the replicate means, which is fitting noise. Centred, \(\kappa = 190\) and the routes give 12.1 and 15.4 digits. A straight line is the right model for a qPCR standard curve (it is what the efficiency formula assumes); higher degree buys nothing but conditioning trouble.



E5. (a bad standard) Back to BCA, mg/mL, \(d = 2\). Drag both standards at 1500 µg/mL up to about 1.60. What happens to the residual signs and the RSS? Raise the degree until the pattern disappears. Does panel (b) change? Press reset points when done.






Answer E5





With both readings near 1.60 the quadratic can no longer follow the data: the RSS jumps from 0.0055 to about 0.14 and the signs form long runs again (+++++++−−−−−−−++−− at exactly 1.600). The residual pattern is gone only at about \(d = 5\) (RSS about 0.003), where the polynomial bends sharply to pass near the two high points. Panel (b) hardly changes: \(\kappa\) depends only on \(A\), that is on the concentrations and the units, not on the readings, and the digits lost by each route stay about the same. The residual plot tells you something is wrong with a standard; raising the degree hides the problem instead of fixing it (repeat the standard).

Then drag the r slider slowly across 2: at 1.99 it still settles at 100, at 2.01 the 2-cycle 112.19/87.81 appears, exactly where |g’(K)| = |1 - r| passes 1. Presets r = 2.3 (2-cycle 159.22/40.78; tick “show g(g(N))” and point at its crossings with the diagonal), 2.6 (4-cycle), 3 (chaos), 3.12 (the 3-cycle window). Then switch to harvested Ricker: from N0 = 30 the stock settles at 74.95, step ratio 0.709 = g’(N); drag N0 down past 20.5 and the stock collapses (N0 = 20: year 13). The lower steady state is repelling, g’ = 1.336, and no start reaches it. Last, the Bisection tab: bracket [50, 100], press step a few times (75, 62.5, 68.75, as on the “Bisection by hand” slide), then +10 steps to 33: width below 1e-8. Click H = 14.26: [0, 50] and [50, 100] have no sign change although two roots 46.22 and 47.28 exist; [40, 47] finds one. That is the double root of “When bisection fails”.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
About this lecture
Measurements come at a few time points; questions are asked in between. This lecture is about drawing one polynomial through all the points, and about when that is a bad idea.

Through n+1 points there is exactly one polynomial of degree \le n. Three ways to write it: monomial (Vandermonde), Lagrange, Newton (divided differences).
The interpolation error has a formula: a derivative of the curve times the node polynomial \prod (t - t_i).
With equally spaced time points, a high degree makes things worse, not better: the Runge phenomenon. Chebyshev points fix it.
Interpolation reproduces noise exactly; with noisy data, fit instead (least squares).
Evaluate with the barycentric formula, not with monomial coefficients.


This opens Part 6. The question is very practical: a plate reader or a sampling schedule gives values at a few times, and we need values in between, for example the OD at the moment an RNA sample was taken. A polynomial through the points is the oldest answer. It works well for a few points close together and fails badly for many points spread out, and the lecture shows both, with the error formula that explains the difference. The practical alternative, piecewise polynomials, is the next lecture, Splines.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
A biology problem first


A culture is read every 2 h (red). RNA was extracted at 3 h and 5 h, between readings. What was the OD then?
The truth is our logistic curve, N(t) = K/(1 + (K/N_0 - 1)e^{-rt}), K = 1.2, N_0 = 0.05, r = 0.8 per hour. In the lab you only have the dots.
The same question for a gene-expression time course: values at 0, 1, 2, 4, 8 h, and you want 3 h.


The running OD curve from Convergence and cost. We use the formula as ground truth so that every error in this lecture can be measured exactly; with real data it cannot be. The blue dashed curve is the degree-4 polynomial through the five readings, and by eye it is almost on the truth. The rest of the lecture asks how good “almost” is, and what happens with more readings over a longer run.

title: Polynomial interpolation
section: One polynomial through all the points
text:
One polynomial through all the points
n+1 readings at distinct times t_0, \dots, t_n → exactly one polynomial p(t) = c_0 + c_1 t + \dots + c_n t^n with p(t_i) = y_i. Two points: a line; three: a parabola.
The conditions p(t_i) = y_i are a square linear system with the Vandermonde matrix:
K <- 1.2; N0 <- 0.05; r <- 0.8
od <- function(t) K / (1 + (K / N0 - 1) * exp(-r * t))
t <- c(0, 2, 4, 6, 8);  y <- od(t)          # 5 readings
V  <- outer(t, 0:4, "^")                    # columns 1, t, t^2, t^3, t^4
cf <- solve(V, y)                           # coefficients c0 ... c4
p  <- function(x) drop(outer(x, 0:4, "^") %*% cf)
p(c(3, 5));  od(c(3, 5))
# [1] 0.4026258 0.8312495                   # interpolant
# [1] 0.3887883 0.8443214                   # truth

Off by +0.014 and −0.013 OD, about 3 %. Not bad for a guess between readings.
This is the polynomial fit of Least squares: normal equations vs QR with as many coefficients as points: the residuals are zero.


Interpolation means the curve passes exactly through every data point. The Vandermonde matrix is the same matrix as in the least-squares lecture, but square now, so solve() gives the unique solution. Uniqueness: if two polynomials of degree n agreed at n+1 points, their difference would be a polynomial of degree n with n+1 roots, so it is zero. The coefficients are not the point; the values in between are. We come back to the danger of this route: with times in hours and many points, V is badly conditioned.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
Lagrange form
Build p from basis polynomials L_i(t) that are 1 at t_i and 0 at every other node:
L_i(t) = \prod_{j \ne i} \frac{t - t_j}{t_i - t_j}, \qquad p(t) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} y_i\, L_i(t).
No linear system to solve. By hand, nodes t = 2, 4, 6, evaluate at t = 3:
L_0(3) = \tfrac{(3-4)(3-6)}{(2-4)(2-6)} = \tfrac{3}{8}, \quad L_1(3) = \tfrac{(3-2)(3-6)}{(4-2)(4-6)} = \tfrac{3}{4}, \quad L_2(3) = \tfrac{(3-2)(3-4)}{(6-2)(6-4)} = -\tfrac{1}{8}
p(3) = \tfrac38(0.2126) + \tfrac34(0.6193) - \tfrac18(1.0090) = 0.4181 \qquad (\text{truth } 0.3888)

The weights L_i(3) add up to 1: interpolating a constant gives the constant back.
A negative weight (-\tfrac18): the value at 3 h is pulled down by the reading at 6 h.


Do this on the board. Each L_i is a product of n linear factors, so it has degree n, it vanishes at every other node, and the denominator makes it 1 at its own node. The sum of y_i L_i then passes through every point. The weights summing to 1 is a good check of hand arithmetic. Negative weights appear as soon as we extrapolate the trend from points further away; with many nodes they become large, and that is where the trouble of this lecture starts. The quadratic misses by 0.03, more than the degree-4 interpolant on the previous slide: here we used only three readings.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
The Lagrange basis


L_i is 1 at its own node and 0 at the others; in between it is free to swing.
Near the ends of the interval the swings are larger. Remember this picture for the Runge slides.


The five basis polynomials for the nodes 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. The interpolant is a weighted sum of these curves with the readings as weights. The basis polynomials of the end nodes (blue and yellow) are small in the middle, but the inner ones swing below zero and above one near the ends. With 13 equispaced nodes the largest of them reaches 18, and any error in the readings is multiplied by them.

title: Polynomial interpolation
Polynomial interpolation
text:
Newton form
Write p so that each new node adds one term:
p(t) = a_0 + a_1(t - t_0) + a_2(t - t_0)(t - t_1) + \dots + a_n(t - t_0)\cdots(t - t_{n-1}).
The coefficients are divided differences: f[t_i] = y_i and
f[t_i, \dots, t_{i+k}] = \frac{f[t_{i+1}, \dots, t_{i+k}] - f[t_i, \dots, t_{i+k-1}]}{t_{i+k} - t_i}, \qquad a_k = f[t_0, \dots, t_k].

f[t_0, t_1] = \dfrac{y_1 - y_0}{t_1 - t_0} is a slope; f[t_0, t_1, t_2] is a change of slope, about f''/2.
In general f[t_0, \dots, t_k] = f^{(k)}(\xi)/k! for some \xi between the nodes: a derivative estimate from data.


The Newton form is built like a Taylor polynomial, but with differences instead of derivatives. Point out that the first divided difference is just the finite-difference slope from Convergence and cost, and the second is half a second derivative. This link (divided difference = scaled derivative at some point) is what gives the error formula two slides on. The recursion is a triangular table, next slide.

The first three terms are the quadratic through 2, 4, 6: 0.4181, as on the Lagrange slide.
The 4th reading added one term (-0.0141) and changed nothing else.


Fill in the table column by column on the board. Each entry is (entry below-left minus entry above-left) divided by the spread of the times it covers. The top diagonal (bold) holds the Newton coefficients. The point to stress is that the quadratic is a sub-sum of the cubic: adding a reading appends one more column and one more term. That is why Newton’s form suits data that arrive one at a time. The cubic is better than the quadratic at 3 h, but not as good as the degree-4 interpolant that also uses the reading at 0 h.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
Newton in R
divdiff <- function(x, y) {           # returns f[x0], f[x0,x1], ..., f[x0..xn]
  n <- length(x); a <- y
  for (k in 2:n)
    for (i in n:k) a[i] <- (a[i] - a[i - 1]) / (x[i] - x[i - k + 1])
  a
}
newton_eval <- function(x, a, xx) {   # nested multiplication, like Horner
  n <- length(a); p <- a[n]
  for (k in (n - 1):1) p <- a[k] + (xx - x[k]) * p
  p
}
newton_eval(t, divdiff(t, y), c(3, 5))
# [1] 0.4026258 0.8312495

The table costs O(n^2) once; each evaluation is then O(n).
Same polynomial again, as it must be.


divdiff overwrites the column in place, running i backwards so that the values still needed are not overwritten yet. newton_eval nests the products: a0 + (t - t0)(a1 + (t - t1)(a2 + …)), the same trick as Horner’s rule for ordinary polynomials. It works with vectors xx directly. In the exercise students build the table by hand and check it with this code.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
How large is the error?
If the true curve f has n+1 derivatives, then for every t there is a \xi between the nodes and t with
f(t) - p(t) = \underbrace{\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}}_{\text{the curve}} \; \underbrace{(t - t_0)(t - t_1)\cdots(t - t_n)}_{\text{node polynomial } w(t):\ \text{the sampling}}

One more derivative than the degree: a polynomial of degree \le n is reproduced exactly (f^{(n+1)} = 0).
w(t) is zero at the nodes and depends only on where you sampled. You control it; you do not control f.
Same shape as Taylor’s remainder (Convergence and cost): Taylor has all n+1 factors equal to (t - t_0).


This is the key formula of the lecture, stated without proof (it follows from Rolle’s theorem applied n+1 times; the textbooks have it in half a page). Read it as a product of two parts. The derivative part is a property of the biology: a smooth curve has modest high derivatives, a sharp switch has huge ones. The node polynomial is a property of the experimental design. We cannot know xi, so in practice we bound the derivative by its maximum. Make the link to Taylor explicit: the Taylor polynomial is the limit where all nodes coincide.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
The error formula with numbers
Linear interpolation between the readings at 2 h and 4 h, at t = 3:
f(3) - p(3) = \frac{f''(\xi)}{2}(3-2)(3-4) = -\frac{f''(\xi)}{2}, \quad f''(3) = 0.0592 \;\Rightarrow\; \approx -0.0296
Actual: p(3) = (0.2126 + 0.6193)/2 = 0.4160, truth 0.3888, error -0.0272. ✓
Degree 4 through t = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, with \max |f^{(5)}| = 0.0983 on [0, 8]:

The bound holds; it is pessimistic because it uses the largest derivative.
The same nodes are 2.3 times worse near the ends: |w| is larger there.


f’‘(3) = 0.0592 is the same second derivative as in Convergence and cost, where it set the error constant of the forward difference. For linear interpolation the error at the midpoint is h^2/8 times f’’, here 4/8 times 0.059 = 0.030. For degree 4 the fifth derivative was computed with R’s D() (the exercise shows how). The actual error at 1 h is left as an exercise. The important observation is in the w column: the node polynomial is larger near the ends. With 5 nodes the factor is 2.3; with 13 nodes it is about 300, next slides.

title: Polynomial interpolation
section: A longer run: 48 h, a reading every 4 h
text:
A longer run: 48 h, a reading every 4 h


13 readings, so a degree-12 interpolant. It passes through every reading, and dips to OD = −0.15 at 0.9 h: a negative cell density.
It also wiggles in stationary phase near 44–48 h. In the middle it is fine.
This is the Runge phenomenon (Carl Runge, 1901).


Same culture, a longer experiment, a typical plate-reader overnight run. Every reading is exact (no noise at all) and the interpolant still produces nonsense between the first two readings. The largest error, 0.25 OD, is right at the start, in lag phase, which is often exactly the part a biologist cares about (lag time). The classic textbook example is Runge’s function 1/(1 + 25 x^2) on [-1, 1], which the exercise reproduces. The cause is the same: equally spaced nodes and a function whose derivatives grow fast.

title: Polynomial interpolation
section: Why the ends? The node polynomial
text:
Why the ends? The node polynomial


Equispaced (red): |w(t)| is about 300 times larger between the first two readings than in the middle.
The error is |f^{(13)}(\xi)|/13! \times |w(t)|: the same derivative factor, multiplied by a much larger w at the ends.
Chebyshev times (blue, ticks on top) are crowded towards the ends, and |w| is level across the whole run.


Log scale on the y axis. Each dip is a node, where w is zero. For equispaced nodes the arches grow towards both ends by orders of magnitude; this is a property of equal spacing, true for any curve. The Chebyshev arches all have the same height: that is the defining property of Chebyshev points, they make the largest value of |w| as small as possible. The derivative part also matters: the logistic has large high derivatives (its complex singularity is close to the steep part), which is why the 0-8 h run did not show the effect.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
More readings make it worse


0–8 h, equispaced (green): error falls with n, by a factor \approx 1.6 per extra reading, until rounding sets in near 10^{-8}.
0–48 h, equispaced (red): error jumps between 0.03 and 0.6 OD and does not converge.
0–48 h, Chebyshev (blue): falls steadily, 2\times10^{-5} at n = 40.


The error-vs-n plot for this method, on a log axis. Green: short interval relative to the curve’s steep part, so the error formula’s derivative factor is beaten by the (n+1)! in the denominator, and the polynomial converges, geometrically. Its upturn after n = 34 is rounding error amplified by the large basis polynomials of equispaced nodes: a second, independent reason to avoid high degree with equal spacing. Red: on the long run the node polynomial wins; the error oscillates and grows for larger n. Blue: the same curve and the same number of readings, only the times moved. Check for students: if adding readings does not reduce the change in your interpolant, you are in the red regime.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
Chebyshev nodes
On [-1, 1]: x_k = \cos\!\left(\dfrac{(2k+1)\pi}{2n+2}\right), k = 0, \dots, n. On [a, b]: t_k = \tfrac{a+b}{2} - \tfrac{b-a}{2}\,x_k.
They are the projections of equally spaced points on a semicircle, so they crowd at the ends.
n <- 12; k <- 0:n
tc <- 24 - 24 * cos((2 * k + 1) * pi / (2 * n + 2))   # 13 times in [0, 48] h
round(tc, 2)
#  [1]  0.17  1.56  4.25  8.09 12.85 18.26 24.00 29.74 35.15 39.91 43.75 46.44
# [13] 47.83

They minimise \max |w(t)|: the smallest possible value is 2\left(\tfrac{b-a}{4}\right)^{n+1}.
For a smooth curve the error then falls geometrically with n.


Draw a semicircle over [-1, 1], mark n+1 equally spaced angles, drop them to the axis. These are Chebyshev points of the first kind, the zeros of the Chebyshev polynomial T_{n+1}; the second kind (extreme points, cos(k pi / n)) includes the endpoints and is equally good. numpy has chebpts1 and chebpts2. Experimental-design reading: sample densely at the beginning and end of the run and sparsely in the middle. That is rarely how anyone designs a growth experiment, which is the honest limitation of this fix.

title: Polynomial interpolation
section: Chebyshev times on the same run
text:
Chebyshev times on the same run


Same 13 readings’ worth of effort, same degree 12. Largest error 0.039 OD instead of 0.25, no negative OD.
In practice you rarely choose the times freely. With the times you have, use low degree, locally: a line between neighbours (approx), or the cubic splines of the next lecture.

approx(t, y, xout = c(3, 5))$y        # piecewise linear, 0-8 h readings
# [1] 0.4159873 0.8141777             # errors 0.027, -0.030

The remaining error of 0.039 is at the end of the steep rise, near 6 h, where Chebyshev points are already sparse; with more Chebyshev points it keeps falling (blue curve two slides back). approx is base R’s piecewise linear interpolation; it can never overshoot the readings, which is its great virtue. Its error is h^2/8 times max |f’’| per interval, from the error formula with n = 1. Splines (next lecture) keep the locality and add smoothness.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
Interpolation vs fitting


Hourly readings over 12 h with plate-reader noise (sd 0.02 OD). The degree-12 interpolant goes through the noise and swings to 0.39 OD off near the ends.
A degree-5 least-squares fit (blue) ignores the noise: error 0.032. Without noise, the interpolant’s error was only 0.008.


Interpolation assumes the readings are exact. Real readings are not. Each reading’s error is multiplied by the corresponding basis polynomial L_i, and for 13 equispaced points the largest single L_i reaches 18 near the ends, and the sum of all |L_i| (the Lebesgue constant) reaches 89; for 13 Chebyshev points it is only 2.6. That turns noise of 0.02 into swings of 0.4. A fit with fewer coefficients than points averages the noise out instead. Choosing the degree of a fit is a bias-variance question; the next lecture, Splines, makes it explicit with smoothing splines.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
Interpolation vs fitting in R
set.seed(1)
t12 <- 0:12                                  # hourly for 12 h
y12 <- od(t12) + rnorm(13, sd = 0.02)        # plate-reader noise
f_int <- lm(y12 ~ poly(t12, 12))             # 13 coefficients: interpolation
f_fit <- lm(y12 ~ poly(t12, 5))              # 6 coefficients: least squares
max(abs(resid(f_int)))
# [1] 0                                       # passes through every point
tt <- seq(0, 12, by = 0.01)
max(abs(predict(f_int, data.frame(t12 = tt)) - od(tt)))
# [1] 0.3937819
max(abs(predict(f_fit, data.frame(t12 = tt)) - od(tt)))
# [1] 0.03161686

poly() builds orthogonal columns (a QR of the Vandermonde matrix), so even degree 12 is well conditioned.
Zero residuals are a warning sign, not a success: the model has as many parameters as data.


lm with as many coefficients as points is interpolation; with fewer it is least squares, exactly as in Least squares: normal equations vs QR. Using poly() rather than raw powers is what makes degree 12 possible at all (next slide). The diagnostic: compare the interpolant with a lower-degree fit; if they differ by much more than the measurement noise between the points, the interpolant is chasing noise.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
Monomial coefficients lose digits

t48 <- seq(0, 48, by = 4)
solve(outer(t48, 0:12, "^"), od(t48))
# Error in solve.default(...) :
#   system is computationally singular: reciprocal condition number = 5.66168e-23

In hours, t^{12} reaches 48^{12} \approx 10^{20}: \kappa(V) \approx 8\times10^{20}, R refuses from n = 9.
Rescaled to [-1, 1] it works longer but stalls at 10^{-5}–10^{-4}: the coefficients carry the rounding errors of an ill-conditioned solve.


Even at Chebyshev nodes, the monomial basis is a bad basis: the Vandermonde matrix’s condition number grows exponentially with n, as in the least-squares lecture. Orange: times in hours, solve gives up already at n = 9. Red: rescaled to [-1, 1] and forced through with tol = 0; the error follows the true interpolation error down to about 1e-5 and then stalls and wanders: kappa(V) reaches 1e18 to 1e19, so the coefficients have essentially no correct digits, and only the cancellation between them keeps the values roughly right. Blue: the same polynomial evaluated with the barycentric formula, which never forms coefficients; it reaches 1e-12. The problem is not the polynomial but how it is represented.

title: Polynomial interpolation
section: The barycentric form: the stable way to evaluate
text:
The barycentric form: the stable way to evaluate
Divide the Lagrange form by the Lagrange form of the constant 1:
p(t) = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_j \frac{w_j\, y_j}{t - t_j}}{\displaystyle\sum_j \frac{w_j}{t - t_j}}, \qquad w_j = \frac{1}{\prod_{k \ne j}(t_j - t_k)} \quad \left(\text{Chebyshev: } w_j = (-1)^j \sin\tfrac{(2j+1)\pi}{2n+2}\right)
bary_weights <- function(x) sapply(seq_along(x), function(j) 1 / prod(x[j] - x[-j]))
bary_eval <- function(x, y, w, xx) sapply(xx, function(z) {
  d <- z - x
  if (any(d == 0)) return(y[d == 0])          # z is a node
  sum(w * y / d) / sum(w / d)
})
bary_eval(t, y, bary_weights(t), c(3, 5))
# [1] 0.4026258 0.8312495

Weights O(n^2) once, then O(n) per point; a new reading updates the weights in O(n).
Rounding errors in numerator and denominator largely cancel: accurate to \approx\varepsilon times the Lebesgue constant. Python: scipy.interpolate.BarycentricInterpolator.


The trick: the weights w_j do not depend on t, and dividing by the same sum for y = 1 makes any common scaling of the weights cancel, which is why the simple Chebyshev formula (scaled weights) works. Higham (2004) proved the formula is numerically stable for nodes with a small Lebesgue constant such as Chebyshev points. This is what serious software does: scipy’s BarycentricInterpolator, and Chebfun in MATLAB, which routinely interpolates with degree 1000 at Chebyshev points. In R there is pracma::barylag; the five lines above are enough. Note the guard for t equal to a node, where the formula would divide by zero.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
Checklist: is my interpolant trustworthy?

Plot it on a fine grid, not only at the readings. Values outside the biology (negative OD, OD above the plateau) → Runge or noise.
Leave one reading out, interpolate from the rest, compare at the left-out time: the difference estimates the error.
Change the degree (drop the end readings, or add one): if the answer between readings changes a lot, do not trust it.
Noisy readings? Do not interpolate: fit (least squares, lower degree) or smooth (Splines).
Never extrapolate a polynomial beyond the first or last reading: |w(t)| grows like |t|^{n+1} outside.
Evaluate stably: barycentric formula or poly(); not solve() on raw powers.


Each item maps to a slide. Item 2 is the practical version of the error formula: with real data we do not know the truth, but leave-one-out tells us how much the answer depends on each reading. Item 5 deserves emphasis: outside the readings every factor of w grows, and a degree-12 polynomial goes to plus or minus infinity like t^12. Extrapolating a growth curve with a polynomial is a common error in lab spreadsheets (Excel’s trendline “polynomial order 6”).

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
Summary

n+1 readings → one interpolating polynomial of degree \le n. Monomial (Vandermonde), Lagrange (\sum y_i L_i) and Newton (divided differences) are three ways to write the same polynomial.
Error: f(t) - p(t) = \dfrac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}\prod (t - t_i): a property of the curve times a property of the sampling.
Equispaced readings: |w| explodes near the ends, so a high degree diverges (Runge): a 48-h run read every 4 h gives a negative OD.
Chebyshev times (crowded at the ends) keep |w| level; the error then falls geometrically.
Readings are noisy: interpolation copies the noise and amplifies it; fit with fewer parameters instead.
Evaluate with the barycentric formula; raw powers of t are badly conditioned.

Next: Splines: low-degree pieces joined smoothly, the practical answer for real sampling times.

Recap the three messages: one polynomial, three representations; the error formula with its two factors; and the practical conclusion that high-degree global polynomials on equispaced or noisy data are a bad idea. The next lecture keeps polynomials but uses them locally: piecewise cubics (splines) through the same readings, and smoothing splines for noisy ones, with the growth rate as the derivative of the smoothed OD curve.

title: Exercise: bisection and fixed-point iteration
text:
Explore
The demo below iterates the population models of this exercise in your browser (\(K = 100\) throughout). The tab Iterate: cobweb shows (a) the cobweb plot of \(g\) with the diagonal \(y = x\) and (b) the same iterates as a time series. Click or drag in the cobweb plot (or use the slider) to set the starting population \(N_0\). Steady states are marked filled (attracting, \(|g'(N^*)| < 1\)) or open (repelling). The readout gives \(g'(N^*)\) at every steady state, the ratio of the last two steps \(d_{n-1}/d_{n-2}\) (Fact 5), and the long-run behaviour after 3000 years: a steady state, a \(k\)-cycle, collapse, or no repeat (chaos). The tab Bisection on f = g − N shows \(f(N) = g(N) - N\) with a starting bracket \([a, b]\) that you can drag. Press step to bisect, and watch the error bound and the actual error of the midpoint in panel (b).



E1. (two steady states, one visible) With the harvested Ricker model (\(r = 0.5\), \(H = 10\)), read both steady states and their \(g'(N^*)\) from the readout. Then use the presets \(N_0 = 30\), \(21\) and \(20\), and drag \(N_0\) slowly between 20 and 21. Which steady state does the iteration reach, and from which starting values? Is there any \(N_0\) from which the iteration converges to the lower steady state?






Answer E1





\(N^* = 74.95\) with \(g' = 0.709\) (attracting, monotone) and \(N^* = 20.48\) with \(g' = 1.336\) (repelling). From \(N_0 = 30\) the stock reaches \(74.941\) after 30 years and settles at \(74.952\); from \(21\) it climbs slowly at first (the cobweb steps away from 20.48) and also settles at \(74.952\). From \(20\) it shrinks: \(\dots, 10.48, 6.40, 0.21\), and it collapses in year 13. Dragging shows the threshold: \(N_0 = 20.5\) survives, \(20.4\) collapses in year 19; the closer \(N_0\) is to \(20.48\), the longer the stock hesitates before it decides. No starting value converges to the lower steady state: every start near it is pushed away, and the cobweb staircase leads away from the open circle on both sides. The lower root is a threshold that iteration can never find; bisection can (E4).



E2. (the rate is \(g'(N^*)\)) Keep \(N_0 = 30\) and 30 years, and compare the step ratio with \(g'\) at the upper steady state. Then switch to Beverton–Holt and use the presets \(R = 2\) and \(R = 3\) (step the years up to 30 with +1 year), and to Ricker with \(r = 0.5\) and \(r = 1.9\). For each, what does the step ratio approach, and how does the cobweb look when the ratio is negative?






Answer E2





Harvested stock: ratio \(0.709\), equal to \(g'(74.95) = 0.709\). Beverton–Holt \(R = 2\): \(0.506\) after 10 years, \(0.500\) after 30, which is \(g'(K) = 1/R\); \(R = 3\): \(0.333 = 1/3\) after 10 years. Ricker \(r = 0.5\): \(0.500 = 1 - r\), a staircase. Ricker \(r = 1.9\): \(-0.900 = 1 - r\); the cobweb is a slowly tightening spiral around \((100, 100)\) and the time series alternates above and below \(K\), still \(0.39\) off after 30 years. The step ratio measures \(g'(N^*)\) without knowing \(N^*\): a negative ratio means alternation, and a ratio near \(\pm 1\) means slow convergence.



E3. (from steady state to cycles to chaos) In the Ricker model, use the presets \(r = 1.5\), \(2.3\), \(2.6\), \(3\) and \(3.12\), and record \(g'(100)\) and the long-run behaviour for each. Then drag the \(r\) slider slowly from \(1.9\) to \(2.1\). At which \(r\) does the steady state \(N^* = 100\) stop attracting? At \(r = 2.3\) tick show g(g(N)): where does that curve cross the diagonal?






Answer E3





\(r = 1.5\): \(g' = -0.5\), settles at 100 (spiral). \(r = 2.3\): \(g' = -1.3\), repelling; a 2-cycle \(159.22, 40.78\). \(r = 2.6\): \(g' = -1.6\); a 4-cycle \(190.48, 18.12, 152.32, 39.08\). \(r = 3\): \(g' = -2\); no repeat within 64 years, chaos. \(r = 3.12\): a 3-cycle \(266.99, 1.46, 31.55\), a window of order inside the chaos. On the slider, \(r = 1.99\) settles at 100, \(r = 2.00\) is still creeping towards 100 after 3000 years (\(g' = -1\) exactly), and \(r = 2.01\) gives the 2-cycle \(112.19, 87.81\): the steady state stops attracting exactly where \(|g'(K)| = |1 - r|\) reaches 1. The curve \(g(g(N))\) crosses the diagonal at 0, 40.78, 100 and 159.22: the two points of the 2-cycle are fixed points of \(g \circ g\) that are not fixed points of \(g\). The steady state \(100\) still exists for every \(r\); it is just never reached.



E4. (bisection, step by step) Open the Bisection tab with the harvested stock and the bracket \([50, 100]\). Press step three times and write down the bracket and the midpoint each time. Then step on to 33 steps: compare the width with \(10^{-8}\) and the actual error with the bound \((b-a)/2\). Keep stepping: what happens in the 40s? Finally, try the brackets \([0, 100]\) and \([0, 50]\).






Answer E4





Midpoint \(75\) with \(f(75) = -0.0139\), so the new bracket is \([50, 75]\); then \(m = 62.5\), \(f = 2.89\), bracket \([62.5, 75]\); then \(m = 68.75\), \(f = 1.63\), bracket \([68.75, 75]\). The first midpoint happened to be within \(0.048\) of the root, but bisection does not know that and keeps halving. After 33 steps the width is \(5.8\times10^{-9} < 10^{-8}\), as the readout predicts (33 steps), and the actual error is \(6.8\times10^{-10}\), below the bound \(2.9\times10^{-9}\). In panel (b) the bound is a straight line (one binary digit per step, rate \(\tfrac12\)); the actual errors wobble below it. In the 40s the bracket reaches a few gaps between doubles near 75 (\(1.7\times10^{-13}\) after 48 steps), \(f(m)\) evaluates to exactly 0, and bisection stops: the floating-point floor. \([0, 100]\): \(f(0) = f(100) = -10\), no sign change, bisection cannot start although two roots lie inside. \([0, 50]\) finds the lower root \(20.482\), the one the iteration in E1 could never reach.



E5. (the double root) Still in the Bisection tab, use the catch buttons \(H = 14\), \(14.26\) and \(15\) with the brackets \([0, 50]\) and \([50, 100]\). Which ones work? At \(H = 14.26\), find a bracket that does work by dragging \(a\) and \(b\) (or use \([40, 47]\)). Then go to the cobweb tab with \(H = 14.26\) and \(H = 15\): what does the stock do, and how fast?






Answer E5





\(H = 14\): roots \(40.07\) (\(g' = 1.079\), repelling) and \(53.55\) (\(g' = 0.924\), attracting); \(f(50) = 0.20 > 0\), so both brackets work. \(H = 14.26\): \(f(0) = f(100) = -14.26\) and \(f(50) = -0.059\), so no bracket among the three has a sign change, but the readout shows two roots, \(46.22\) and \(47.28\): \(f\) is positive only on that interval of width 1.06, with a maximum of \(0.0016\). \([40, 47]\) works (\(f(47) = +0.0013\)) and finds \(46.22\). The maximum sustainable catch is \(14.2616\) at \(N = 46.75\); at \(H = 15\) there is no root at all. In the cobweb tab at \(H = 14.26\) from \(N_0 = 60\), the stock is still at \(48.33\) after 100 years with step ratio \(0.98\): the attracting root has \(g' = 0.994\), so convergence is very slow, and the repelling root \(46.22\) (the collapse threshold) is only 1 below. At \(H = 15\) the stock collapses (year 35 from \(N_0 = 60\)). Near a double root both methods struggle: bisection cannot find a bracket, and iteration is slow because \(g' \to 1\).

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: Try it: Newton in the plane
text:
Try it: Newton in the plane




The toggle switch with alpha = 3, n = 2, computed live in the browser. Blue and red solid curves: the nullclines F1 = 0 and F2 = 0; the dots are the three steady states. The orange dot is the start (3, 0.5). Click “+ 1”: the two dashed lines are the nullclines of the linear approximation at x0, each one straight; they cross at x1 = (2.6699, 0.3594), exactly the step by hand from earlier. Point at the readout: F = (-0.6, -0.2), J, det J = 0.654, delta = solve(J, -F). Keep clicking: the dashed lines hug the curves more and more, and the errors 0.4, 0.057, 2.1e-3, 2.9e-6, 5.9e-12 show the doubling exponent. Then click (1, 0.2): the first step jumps to the V-high state. Click (1.9, 0.5): det J = -0.03, the dashed lines are nearly parallel, x1 is off the plot at (-5.1, 4.4). Tick “basins”: 21 / 57 / 21 percent as in the figure; tick “det J = 0” and show that the thin bands follow the dotted curve. Finally drag alpha down to 2: the three states merge, the whole square becomes one colour, and the run from (3, 0.5) needs 39 steps because J is singular at the root. That leads into the next slide.

title: Exercise: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Explore
The demo below runs Newton on the toggle switch in your browser. The plot shows the \((u, v)\) plane with the two nullclines \(F_1 = 0\) (blue) and \(F_2 = 0\) (red); the steady states are where they cross (green: U high, white: middle, purple: V high). Click or drag in the plot to move the start \(\mathbf x_0\) (orange). The thin dashed grey line is the whole Newton path; the step buttons walk along it. At the current iterate \(\mathbf x_k\) the two dashed coloured lines are the linearised nullclines, \(F_i(\mathbf x_k) + J_i(\mathbf x_k)\,\boldsymbol\delta = 0\) (row \(i\) of Fact 3 set to zero): straight lines that touch the curved ones near \(\mathbf x_k\). Where they cross is the solution of \(J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F\), the next iterate (yellow dot). The readout gives \(\mathbf F\), \(J\), \(\det J\) and \(\boldsymbol\delta\) at \(\mathbf x_k\), where the run ends, and the error \(\|\mathbf x_k - \mathbf x^*\|\) of every iterate. The run stops when \(\|\mathbf F\| < 10^{-12}\) or after 50 steps.
basins colours every start by the steady state Newton reaches from it (black: no convergence), computed on a grid, and gives the shares for starts in \([0, 4]^2\), as in the lecture’s basin figure. det J = 0 draws the dotted curve where the Jacobian is singular. The sliders change \(\alpha\) and \(n\).



E1. (linearise, solve, repeat) Click the start (3, 0.5) and + 1 once. Read \(\mathbf F\), \(J\), \(\det J\), \(\boldsymbol\delta\) and \(\mathbf x_1\) and compare with the lecture’s step by hand. Where do the two dashed lines cross? Keep clicking + 1 until the run stops. How many steps does it take, and how do the errors per step show quadratic convergence?






Answer E1





\(\mathbf F(\mathbf x_0) = (-0.6, -0.2)\), \(J = \begin{pmatrix}-1 & -1.92\\ -0.18 & -1\end{pmatrix}\), \(\det J = 0.654\), \(\boldsymbol\delta = (-0.330073, -0.140587)\), \(\mathbf x_1 = (2.669927, 0.359413)\): the same as by hand. The dashed lines cross exactly at \(\mathbf x_1\): each dashed line is where one component of the linear approximation is zero, so their crossing is where both are, the solution of \(J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F\). Near the “U high” state the dashed lines lie almost on top of the curves, so their crossing is almost the root. The run ends at \((2.618034, 0.381966)\) after 5 steps, with errors \(0.400\), \(0.0566\), \(2.1\times10^{-3}\), \(2.9\times10^{-6}\), \(5.9\times10^{-12}\), \(\approx 0\): the exponent roughly doubles each step.



E2. (which root?) Click the starts (1, 0.2) and (1, 1) and step through each. Where does each run end, and why? Then tick basins. What shares do you read for starts in \([0, 4]^2\)? Drag the start slowly from \((1, 0.2)\) to the right along \(v = 0.2\): where does the answer switch to “U high”?






Answer E2





From \((1, 0.2)\) the first step jumps to \((0.334, 2.499)\) and the run ends in V high \((0.381966, 2.618034)\) after 5 steps, although \(u > v\) at the start: the crossing of the linearised nullclines happens to lie up on the left. From \((1, 1)\) every iterate stays on the diagonal (\((1.2, 1.2)\) after one step, B8) and the run ends in the middle state \((1.213412, 1.213412)\) after 4 steps. The basin shares are U high 21 %, middle 57 %, V high 21 %, no convergence 0 %, as in the lecture: the unstable middle state is Newton’s most common answer. Along \(v = 0.2\) the start stays in the purple (V high) region up to \(u \approx 1.4\); between about \(1.45\) and \(1.55\) the answer flips between middle, U high and V high in a thin band, and from \(u \approx 1.6\) on the run ends in U high. The boundaries are curved and have nothing to do with the diagonal \(u = v\) that separates the cell’s two fates.



E3. (a nearly singular Jacobian) Click (1.9, 0.5) and + 1. Read \(\det J\) and \(\mathbf x_1\), then follow the run to the end. Do the same for (2, 0.55). Now tick det J = 0. Where do the two starts lie relative to the dotted curve, and what does the basin picture look like near it?






Answer E3





At \((1.9, 0.5)\): \(\det J = -0.0299\) (“nearly singular”); the dashed lines are almost parallel, so they cross far away: \(\mathbf x_1 = (-5.14, 4.43)\), off the plot, with a negative concentration. From there the run comes back and ends in the middle state after 7 steps. At \((2, 0.55)\): \(\det J = 0.0663\), \(\mathbf x_1 = (5.106, -0.891)\), also a huge step, but it ends in U high after 7 steps. Both starts lie just on either side of the dotted curve \(\det J = 0\). Along that curve the basins break into thin interleaved bands of all three colours: a tiny change of the start sends the first step to a very different place.



E4. (bistability needs \(\alpha > 2\)) Keep basins on, start at (3, 0.5), and lower \(\alpha\): \(2.5\), \(2.2\), \(2.05\), \(2\), \(1.5\). For each, count the steady states and read the shares. Compare the “U high” state with \(u = (\alpha + \sqrt{\alpha^2 - 4})/2\) from B5. What is special about \(\alpha = 2\): the number of steps, the errors per step, and the black area?






Answer E4

The U-high states agree with \((\alpha + \sqrt{\alpha^2-4})/2\): \(2\), \(1.5583\), \(1.25\). As \(\alpha \to 2\) the three states move together and at \(\alpha = 2\) they merge at \((1, 1)\), where \(\det J = 0\): the Jacobian is singular at the root. From \((3, 0.5)\) the run then needs 39 steps instead of 5–8, and the errors per step shrink only by a factor of about \(2/3\) (\(0.67\), \(0.44\), \(0.28\), …): linear, not quadratic, convergence, like Newton at a multiple root in one variable. The 7 % black starts are runs that are still crawling after 50 steps. Below \(\alpha = 2\) there is one state, the circuit is no switch, and every start finds it.



E5. (the Hill coefficient) Reset, then set \(n = 2.5\) (with \(\alpha = 3\)) and click (2, 0.5). What happens after one step, and why? Tick basins: how large is the black area now? Finally set \(n = 1\) and try \(\alpha\) between 1 and 5. Is the switch ever bistable?






Answer E5





With \(n = 2.5\) the first step from \((2, 0.5)\) goes to \((9.72, -3.25)\); then \(v^{2.5}\) of a negative number is NaN, and the run ends with NaN after 1 step (the lecture’s Failure 1). The steady states still exist (“U high” at \((2.955096, 0.187363)\)), but the shares are U high 16 %, middle 33 %, V high 16 %, no convergence 34 %: every start whose path visits negative concentrations fails. With \(n = 1\) there is a single steady state for every \(\alpha\) (at \(\alpha = 3\): \(u = v = 1.302776\)): without cooperativity no bistability. The black regions there are runs that wander around the poles at \(u = -1\) or \(v = -1\), where \(1 + u^n = 0\).

title: Exercise: Newton and secant methods
text:
Explore
The demo below runs Newton, secant or bisection in your browser on the three equations of the lecture: the two-site dose–response \(f(c) = R(c) - 0.5\), the score \(S(\lambda)\) of the zero-truncated Poisson counts, and Michaelis–Menten in log substrate, \(\sigma(u) - \tfrac12\) (Newton step \(u - \sinh u\)). Drag or click in the plot to move the start value (two start values for secant, the bracket \([a, b]\) for bisection). Step takes one step and draws the tangent (Newton), the chord through the last two points (secant) or the halved bracket (bisection), and where it meets zero; Run keeps stepping, Back undoes a step. The table lists each iterate, \(f\) there, the error against the wanted root (\(c_{50}\), \(\hat\lambda\) or \(u^* = 0\)), the number of correct digits \(-\log_{10}\big(|e|/\max(|x^*|, 1)\big)\), and how the digit count changed from the previous step (multiplied for Newton and secant, added for bisection). The digits of \(x_k\) that agree with the root are in bold. The demo stops like the lecture’s newton() and secant(): when a step is below \(10^{-12}\,|x|\), or after 60 steps.
The browser computes in the same IEEE doubles as R and Python, but exp and log may round differently in the last bit, so the last digit of an iterate can differ from the lecture.



E1. (digits double) Click Newton c₀ = 1 and press Step five times. After each step, write down the error, the number of correct digits and the “× digits” factor. Watch the tangent of each step in the plot. How far is \(c_1\) from the root, and why is the first step still a big improvement? How many function evaluations did the run take?






Answer E1





Errors \(3.6\times10^{-1}\), \(6.5\times10^{-3}\), \(1.6\times10^{-6}\), \(9.1\times10^{-14}\), \(4.4\times10^{-16}\); correct digits \(1.0\), \(2.7\), \(6.3\), \(13.6\), all. From step 2 on the digit count is multiplied by about 2 each step (\(2.8\), \(2.3\), \(2.1\)): quadratic convergence. The bold part of \(c_k\) grows the same way. The first tangent, drawn at \(c_0 = 1\) where the curve is still flat and bending, overshoots to \(c_1 = 3.617\), \(0.36\) past the root; but the error fell from \(2.3\) to \(0.36\), and from there the tangent is a good model of the curve. The run stops after 5 steps with 10 evaluations (\(f\) and \(f'\) at each of \(c_0, \ldots, c_4\)), as in the lecture.



E2. (secant and bisection) Click secant 1, 2 and Run. Record the correct digits per step and the factors, the number of steps and of evaluations. Then click bisection [1, 10] and press Step ten times, recording the digits, then Run to the end. Which method needs the fewest evaluations of \(f\) for full precision?






Answer E2





Secant: digits \(1.3\), \(3.2\), \(5.3\), \(9.4\), all; factors \(2.4\), \(1.7\), \(1.8\), close to the golden ratio \(1.618\). It stops after 6 steps (the sixth step is too small to change \(c\)) with 8 evaluations: 2 for the start values and one per step. Bisection: digits \(0.2\), \(2.5\), \(0.5\), \(0.8\), \(1.1\), \(1.4\), \(1.7\), \(2.1\), \(2.7\), \(3.1\): about \(+0.3\) per step, with a lucky hit at step 2 (\(c = 3.25\)) that is lost again at step 3. Bisection needs 42 steps and 44 evaluations. Per evaluation the secant method (8) beats Newton (10 in E1), and both beat bisection by a factor of about 5.



E3. (the MLE and a bad start) Choose MLE from x̄ = 1.73 and Run. Read the digits and factors. Then drag \(\lambda_0\) to the right, in steps of 0.01, and find the largest start from which Newton still reaches \(\hat\lambda\). Finally click 2 bad start (\(\lambda_0 = 3\)) and Step through it. What happens to \(\lambda_k\), and how does the run end?






Answer E3





From \(\bar x = 1.73\): digits \(0.9\), \(1.8\), \(3.6\), \(7.2\), \(14.5\), all, with factors \(2.1\), \(2.0\), \(2.0\), \(2.0\): textbook quadratic convergence. 6 steps, 12 evaluations, \(\hat\lambda = 1.218469525830127\). The last start that works is \(\lambda_0 = 2.70\): its first tangent lands at \(\lambda_1 = 0.0056\), just right of 0, and Newton crawls back in 15 steps. From \(2.71\) on, \(\lambda_1 < 0\) (\(-0.009\) for \(2.71\)) and the run fails, in line with the lecture (“up to about 2.7”). From \(\lambda_0 = 3\): \(\lambda_1 = -0.47\) (the demo warns: negative rate), then \(-1.07\), \(-2.59\), \(-6.03\), \(-12.3\), \(-24.7\), …: each step roughly doubles \(\lambda\), because for negative \(\lambda\) the score behaves like \(173/\lambda\). At \(\lambda_{11} = -789\), \(e^{-\lambda}\) overflows, and \(\lambda_{12}\) is NaN: diverged.



E4. (a flat tangent) Click 1 flat tangent (\(c_0 = 10\)) and Run. Where does \(c_1\) land, what root does the run converge to, and what do the columns \(f(c_k)\), error and digits say at the end? Then drag \(c_0\) from \(6\) to \(12\) and watch where the runs end. Finally switch to bisection with \([a, b] = [1, 10]\).






Answer E4





\(f'(10)\) is small, so the tangent at \(c_0 = 10\) is nearly flat and meets zero at \(c_1 = -5.73\). Newton then converges in 6 steps to \(c = -3.04997\): the status says converged, \(f(c_k)\) drops to \(10^{-16}\), but the error against \(c_{50}\) stays at \(6.3\) and the digits at \(0\): a confident, wrong, negative dose. Dragging \(c_0\): every start up to \(7.85\) reaches \(c_{50}\). Above that the outcome jumps around: \(c_0 = 7.9\)–\(8.0\) ends at a second negative root, \(c = -0.2513\) (right of the pole at \(c = -0.1\)); \(8.05\)–\(8.2\) comes back to \(c_{50}\); \(8.25\) and \(8.3\) run off to \(-10^{300}\) and end in NaN; from \(8.35\) to \(10.3\) every start ends at \(-3.05\); most starts between \(10.4\) and \(11.15\) reach \(c_{50}\) again, and from \(11.35\) on the iterates run off to \(-\infty\). Nothing in Newton’s output warns you; only a range check does. Bisection on \([1, 10]\) cannot leave the bracket and always ends at \(c_{50}\), at the price of 44 evaluations.



E5. (cycling) Click 3 cycling (\(u_0 = 2.1773189849653\), \(S_0 = 8.82\,K_m\)) and Run. The demo pauses when it detects a cycle. Look at the late digits of \(u_k\) in the table, then press Run again and let it finish. Then drag \(u_0\) to \(2.30\) and to \(1.61\) (\(S_0 = 10\,K_m\) and \(5\,K_m\)).






Answer E5





The tangents bounce between \(u = 2.177\) and \(-2.177\) (\(S = 8.82\,K_m\) and \(K_m/8.82\)), and the demo pauses at step 3 with a cycling warning. The late digits are not constant: \(2.17731898496530\), \(\ldots 65228\), \(\ldots 64363\), \(\ldots 53958\): the distance from the exact cycle grows about 12-fold every two steps, because the cycle is unstable and the start is only correct to 13 digits. In this browser the iterates leave the cycle after about 25 steps and then converge to \(u = 0\) at step 31; whether a run escapes towards the root or towards infinity depends on the rounding, so R may behave differently. From \(u_0 = 2.30\) each step lands farther out: \(-2.64\), \(4.31\), \(-33.0\), \(1.1\times10^{14}\), then \(-\infty\): diverged. From \(u_0 = 1.61\): converged in 5 steps. In 0.01 steps the last start that converges is \(u_0 = 2.17\); from \(2.18\) on, Newton diverges. A cap on the number of steps (and printing the last iterates) is what turns an endless bounce into a message.

section: Try it: step through Newton, secant and bisection
text:
Try it: step through Newton, secant and bisection




The same f(c) = R(c) - 0.5, computed live in the browser. Press Step five times from c0 = 1: each step draws the tangent and where it meets zero; the table shows correct digits 1.0, 2.7, 6.3, 13.6, all, the “x digits” column about 2, and the bold digits of c_k grow the same way. 10 evaluations. Click “secant 1, 2” and Run: digits 1.3, 3.2, 5.3, 9.4, all, factors near 1.6; 8 evaluations. Click “bisection [1, 10]” and Run: +0.3 digits per step, 42 steps, 44 evaluations. Then, as a lead-in to the next three slides, click “1 flat tangent” and step: c1 = -5.73, and the run converges to -3.05 with f = 0 and zero correct digits. Drag the start to show that 7.85 still works and 9 does not. The exercise’s Explore section has the bad-start and cycling presets as tasks; show them here only if there is time.
